headline: What a Saudi factory would actually deploy if industrial AI worked
deck: Vision inspection, predictive maintenance and scheduling are the three applications that pay. Everything else on a summit stage is a slide.
excerpt: The Global AI Summit will present artificial intelligence across health, finance, energy and cities. On a factory floor the applications that earn their cost are narrow, and the barrier to each is data rather than algorithms.
content:
The Global AI Summit in Riyadh this week covers artificial intelligence across health, finance, energy and smart cities. The industrial case is quieter and more testable, and it comes down to three applications that have repeatedly paid for themselves in manufacturing plants worldwide.

The first is visual inspection. A camera and a trained model examining every part coming off a line does a job that human inspectors do inconsistently and cannot do at full rate. It catches defects earlier, which reduces the cost of scrapping, and it produces a record of what was inspected. The barrier is not the model but the images: a system trained on a thousand good parts and five defective ones will not recognise the sixth defect type, and collecting defect examples means either waiting for failures or manufacturing them deliberately.

The second is predictive maintenance on rotating equipment. Vibration and thermal data from motors, pumps, compressors and gearboxes, analysed for the signatures that precede failure, converts a breakdown into a planned intervention. The economics are strongest where the equipment is critical and the downtime cost is high, which describes most process industry and much of heavy manufacturing.

The third is scheduling and yield. A plant with many products, changeovers and constraints has a scheduling problem that humans solve adequately and not optimally, and the gains from solving it better are small percentages on large volumes.

What these three have in common is that each replaces a specific judgement with a model validated against a measurable outcome. What they also have in common is that each depends on data the plant may not have. Most industrial data was collected for control, not for analysis: it is sampled at the wrong rate, stored for the wrong duration, unlabelled, and split across systems that were never designed to be joined.

That is the practical constraint on industrial artificial intelligence in the Kingdom, and it is unglamorous. A factory that wants predictive maintenance usually needs sensors, a historian, network coverage on the plant floor and someone to label failures before any model is useful. The instrumentation is the project; the model is the last step.

The connection to the week's larger announcements is real but indirect. National compute capacity trains models; it does not instrument a factory. The Kingdom's industrial base — 39 industrial cities and more than 9,000 facilities under the Saudi Authority for Industrial Cities and Technology Zones — is where the returns would be realised, and getting there is a sensors-and-networks programme before it is an artificial intelligence one.

The summit runs from 15 to 17 September.
author: Jakson Gudawela
scheduledReason: Written before the Global AI Summit opens in Riyadh on 15 September. It works from published announcements and verified infrastructure data, and makes no claim about anything said at the event.
